title.raw: Why a Standalone ER is Faster for Busy Irving Families
title.rendered: Why a Standalone ER is Faster for Busy Irving Families

content.raw:
When a sudden injury or illness strikes, the hardest part is often deciding where to go and how quickly you will be seen. For many Irving and Las Colinas families, a freestanding emergency room offers fast access to emergency-level care, day or night.

This guide explains what a freestanding ER is, what it can treat, and how to decide when your symptoms call for emergency care.

What Is a Freestanding Emergency Room?

A freestanding emergency room is a fully licensed, 24/7 emergency facility that operates on its own rather than inside a larger medical campus. In Texas, these centers are regulated under Health & Safety Code Chapter 254A and are staffed by experienced emergency physicians. They accept walk-in patients with no appointment needed.

A freestanding ER is equipped to evaluate and stabilize true emergencies. On-site CT scans, X-rays, ultrasound, and a laboratory let the care team diagnose and begin treatment quickly. If a patient needs to be admitted or needs surgery, the team arranges a transfer to a partner facility.

What a Freestanding ER Can Treat

Americans make more than 155 million emergency department visits each year, according to the CDC. Freestanding emergency rooms handle the full range of these emergencies, including:

  • Chest pain or possible heart attack symptoms
  • Stroke symptoms such as face drooping, arm weakness, or speech difficulty, the CDC F.A.S.T. warning signs
  • Difficulty breathing or severe shortness of breath
  • Severe abdominal pain
  • High fevers, especially in infants and young children
  • Deep cuts, broken bones, and head injuries
  • Severe allergic reactions

For minor problems like a mild cold, a small rash, or a simple cut, urgent care or a primary care visit is usually the right level of care. A freestanding ER is for problems that could threaten life, limb, or long-term health.

When Should You Go to the ER?

According to MedlinePlus, you should seek emergency care right away for:

  • Chest pain or pressure
  • Difficulty breathing
  • Sudden confusion, weakness, or trouble speaking
  • Uncontrolled bleeding or deep lacerations
  • High fevers that do not respond to medication, especially in infants
  • Serious head injuries or loss of consciousness

For anything life-threatening, such as chest pain, stroke symptoms, or trouble breathing, call 911 first. Paramedics can begin care on the way.

What to Expect During Your Visit

When you arrive, a nurse and physician evaluate you quickly to understand your symptoms. Because labs and imaging are on site, blood work and scans can often be done without leaving the building, so the team can move from diagnosis to treatment without delay.

If you are facing a possible emergency in Irving or Las Colinas, ER of Irving is open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Call (972) 893-3148 or walk in any time.

FAQs

Is a freestanding ER the same as urgent care?

No. Urgent care treats minor illnesses and injuries. A freestanding ER is equipped for life-threatening emergencies, with on-site imaging and lab testing.

Do you treat children?

Yes. Pediatric emergencies are common, and the team is equipped to care for children of all ages.

Can I get a CT scan or X-ray there?

Yes. On-site CT, X-ray, and ultrasound are available 24/7, along with full laboratory testing.

What should I bring with me?

If you can, bring a photo ID, your insurance card, and a list of your current medications. Do not delay care to find them.

Do I need insurance to be seen?

No. Federal law (EMTALA) requires every emergency room to evaluate and stabilize you regardless of insurance or ability to pay.

title.raw: Recognizing Sepsis: When an Infection Becomes Deadly
title.rendered: Recognizing Sepsis: When an Infection Becomes Deadly

content.raw:
Sepsis is a life-threatening emergency that starts with an ordinary infection. A cold, a UTI, or even a small skin scrape can set it off. The infection triggers a chain reaction that harms your own organs.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), at least 1.7 million adults in America develop sepsis each year. Most people survive when the warning signs are caught early and treated fast.

This guide covers the red flags, who is most at risk, and what to do the moment you suspect sepsis. If you already see severe symptoms, get emergency sepsis care or call 911 now.

What is Sepsis? Understanding Your Body's Extreme Response

Sepsis is not "blood poisoning" the way many people think. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) defines it as your body's extreme immune response to an infection you already have.

Normally, your immune system fights germs locally. In sepsis, that response goes into overdrive and causes inflammation through your whole body. The inflammation can damage tissue, shut down organs, and turn deadly without fast treatment.

Think of a campfire that jumps its ring and becomes a forest fire. The fire was meant to help. Now it is too large for the body to control.

Sepsis Symptoms: How to Spot the Red Flags Early

Early recognition is the single most important factor in surviving sepsis. It often looks like a "bad flu" at first. The difference is that sepsis symptoms are more intense and get worse by the hour.

The Sepsis Red-Flag Checklist

The CDC lists these warning signs. An infection plus any one of them is an emergency:

  • High heart rate or a weak pulse. As blood pressure drops, the heart pumps faster to compensate. A racing heart while you rest is a serious warning.
  • Fever, shivering, or feeling very cold. Uncontrollable shivering, called rigors, is common. Some patients instead run a very low body temperature.
  • Confusion or unusual sleepiness. The brain is not getting enough oxygen-rich blood. A person may be hard to wake or seem "not themselves."
  • Shortness of breath. MedlinePlus notes the body breathes faster to balance rising acid levels in the blood.
  • Extreme pain or discomfort. Many survivors describe it as the worst pain they have ever felt.
  • Clammy, sweaty, pale, or mottled skin. The body pulls blood away from the skin to protect vital organs.

Trust your instincts too. If you catch yourself saying "I feel like I might die" or "I have never felt this sick," take that seriously. Sepsis survivors report that exact feeling often.

Who is Most at Risk for Sepsis?

Anyone can get sepsis. The CDC reports these groups face the highest risk:

  • Adults 65 or older. Immune systems naturally weaken with age.
  • Children under age 1. Their immune systems are still developing.
  • People with weakened immune systems. This includes chemotherapy patients and people living with HIV.
  • People with chronic conditions. Diabetes, lung disease, cancer, and kidney disease all raise the risk.
  • Anyone recently hospitalized. Surgical wounds and hospital stays open the door to healthcare-associated infections.

From Infection to Emergency: How Sepsis Progresses

Sepsis usually begins with an infection in the lungs, urinary tract, gut, or skin. Pneumonia and UTIs are among the most common starting points. Trouble begins when the infection triggers a body-wide response.

Untreated sepsis can progress to septic shock. In septic shock, blood pressure drops to dangerous lows and organs like the kidneys, liver, and heart begin to shut down. That is why emergency teams call sepsis a race against time.

Why Getting to the ER Fast Matters

The risk of death rises with every hour treatment is delayed. Emergency teams treat sepsis with rapid IV antibiotics and IV fluids. The sooner they start, the better the odds.

You do not need to memorize the treatment details. You just need to get there fast. Our sepsis emergency treatment page explains what our team does the moment you arrive.

What to Do If You Suspect Sepsis

If an infection is not improving, or suddenly gets much worse, do not wait it out.

  1. Get emergency care immediately. Go to the nearest emergency room or call 911.
  2. Say the word "sepsis." Ask the provider directly, "Could this be sepsis?" That question can trigger a rapid treatment protocol.
  3. Track the timeline. Note when the shivering, confusion, or racing heart began. That timing helps the medical team.

An infection paired with a racing heart, high fever, shivering, or confusion is an emergency. Get emergency sepsis care at ER of Irving or call 911 right away.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is sepsis contagious?

No, sepsis itself is not contagious. However, the infection that triggers sepsis, like the flu, pneumonia, or a skin infection, can be passed to others.

Can you have sepsis without a fever?

Yes. While a high fever is common, some people may actually have a lower-than-normal body temperature. This happens most often in the elderly and in advanced sepsis.

What is the difference between sepsis and septicemia?

"Septicemia" is an older term for bacteria in the blood. Sepsis is the broader, more accurate term for the body's overwhelming response to any infection, whether bacterial, viral, or fungal.

How long does it take to recover from sepsis?

Recovery varies. Many people return to normal life within weeks. Some experience Post-Sepsis Syndrome, which includes muscle weakness, fatigue, and anxiety.

Can a simple cut cause sepsis?

Yes. Any opening in the skin can let bacteria enter. If a wound turns red, swollen, or painful and you start shivering or your heart races, seek help immediately.

Sepsis moves fast, but so can you. Learn the red flags, trust your gut, and act at the first sign of trouble.

title.raw: Kidney Stone Pain Relief: When Home Remedies Fail
title.rendered: Kidney Stone Pain Relief: When Home Remedies Fail

content.raw:
The pain of a kidney stone can arrive suddenly and feel overwhelming. Many patients describe it as some of the worst pain they have known. Your first instinct is often to drink more water and reach for a heating pad.

Home care helps many small stones pass on their own. Some stones get stuck, though, and that is when waiting becomes risky. This guide covers which home remedies for kidney stone pain actually help, and when they are not enough.

Staying well hydrated is the foundation of both prevention and relief. You can read more in our guide to dehydration treatment in Irving.

Why "Waiting It Out" Is Not Always the Answer

Most people increase their fluids at the first sign of a stone. The NIDDK recommends six to eight glasses of water a day to help flush the urinary tract.

Hydration is not a cure once a stone is already moving. A stone lodged in the ureter makes the kidney swell and triggers intense spasms. This pattern of pain is called renal colic.

Renal colic comes in waves that last about 20 to 60 minutes. The pain spikes as the ureter squeezes, then eases as it relaxes. That brief relief can feel like the stone has passed when it has not.

Is It a Kidney Stone, or Something Else?

Kidney stone pain usually starts in the flank, the area on your back and side below the ribs. It often moves toward the lower abdomen and groin as the stone travels.

This pain feels deep, and it does not ease when you rest or change position. A simple back strain usually feels different and changes when you stretch.

Several symptoms signal that a stone has become serious. For the full symptom checklist and what our team looks for, see our kidney stone emergency treatment page.

Home Remedies for Kidney Stone Pain: What Actually Helps

A few simple measures can ease discomfort while a small stone passes. None of them replace medical care if your pain becomes severe.

Hydration

Water is the most useful tool you have at home. Aim for pale, nearly clear urine through the day. Good hydration helps a small stone move along.

Heat therapy

A heating pad on your back or flank can relax the muscles around the ureter. Warmth may soften the intensity of a pain wave. Use it for about 20 minutes at a time.

Gentle movement

Light walking may help gravity move a stone lower. Rest if activity sharply increases your pain. Never push through severe or worsening symptoms.

Diet and citrate

Citrate from lemon or lime juice may slow new crystals from forming. Lower salt intake also helps reduce calcium in the urine. These steps support prevention more than fast relief.

Safe Over-the-Counter Pain Relief, and What to Avoid

Over-the-counter medicine can take the edge off mild stone pain. Always follow the dosing on the label. Ask your pharmacist if you take other medicines.

Anti-inflammatory drugs like ibuprofen or naproxen target swelling in the ureter. They often work better than acetaminophen for this pain. Take them with food and water.

Avoid anti-inflammatories if you have kidney disease, ulcers, or take blood thinners. Acetaminophen is a gentler choice in those cases. Stop home medicine and seek care if the pain breaks through.

Why Home Remedies Fall Short for Larger Stones

Popular remedies like apple cider vinegar or olive oil are not proven to dissolve stones. Citrate from lemon can help prevent new crystals, but it will not shrink a stone you already have.

Stone size is the deciding factor. Stones smaller than 4mm pass on their own about 80 percent of the time. Once a stone reaches 6mm or larger, that chance drops sharply.

A wide stone is too large for the narrow ureter, no matter how much water you drink. At that point, home relief only delays the care you need.

A doctor can measure a stone's exact size and location with imaging. A low-dose CT scan is the gold standard for diagnosis, per NIDDK. That is one reason severe or lasting pain needs an in-person evaluation.

Red Flags: When to Stop Home Care and Go to the ER

Some symptoms mean a stone may be blocked or infected. A fever with urinary pain can point to urosepsis, a dangerous infection, per MedlinePlus. Do not wait these out.

Go to an emergency room right away if you have any of the following:

  1. Fever over 101.5°F or chills: a sign of possible infection.
  2. Inability to urinate: a sign of complete blockage.
  3. Uncontrolled vomiting: you cannot keep down fluids or pain medicine.
  4. Heavy bleeding or blood clots in the urine.
  5. Confusion or extreme fatigue: signs of a whole-body problem.

ER of Irving treats kidney stone emergencies 24/7 with on-site imaging and IV pain relief. Call us now at (972) 893-3148.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the fastest way to relieve kidney stone pain at home?

Drink water, apply a heating pad, and take an anti-inflammatory if it is safe for you. These steps ease mild pain. Severe pain needs medical care.

How long does it usually take to pass a kidney stone?

A small stone can take a few days to a few weeks to pass. If it has not passed within four weeks, doctors usually recommend treatment. Waiting longer risks kidney damage.

Does drinking more water make a stone pass faster?

Good hydration helps small stones move through the urinary tract. It will not push out a stone that is too large. Size decides whether a stone can pass.

Is flank pain always a kidney stone?

Not always. Flank pain can also come from a kidney infection, a muscle strain, or shingles. A sudden, severe wave of pain is more typical of a stone.

Can I prevent kidney stones from coming back?

Yes. The NIH suggests drinking enough to make about 2 liters of urine a day. Lower salt intake also helps reduce calcium in your urine.

Home remedies can carry you through a small, uncomplicated stone. Hydration, heat, and safe pain relief all help. Know the red flags so you can act fast when they appear.

If your pain turns severe, or a fever starts, get care without delay. See our kidney stone emergency treatment page, or learn about dehydration treatment in Irving.

Follow ER of Irving on Facebook and Instagram for practical health tips.

content.raw:
Whether it’s a Friday night football game at Irving Schools Stadium or a weekend soccer tournament at Northwest Park, sports are the heartbeat of our community. But as any parent or coach knows, with high energy comes the risk of injury. When a student-athlete takes a hard hit to the head or a jolt to the body, the immediate aftermath can be overwhelming. You might wonder: Is it just a bump, or is it something more? Understanding the concussion symptoms and the proper medical steps to take isn't just about following school rules; it's about protecting your child’s developing brain and their future.

What Exactly Is a Concussion?

A concussion is a type of traumatic brain injury (TBI) caused by a bump, blow, or jolt to the head or by a hit to the body that causes the head and brain to move rapidly back and forth. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), this sudden movement can cause the brain to bounce around or twist in the skull, creating chemical changes in the brain and sometimes stretching and damaging brain cells. Unlike a broken arm, a concussion is an "invisible" injury. You can’t see a concussion on the outside, and symptoms may not appear for hours or even days after the initial impact.

Recognizing Concussion Symptoms in Student-Athletes

As a parent or coach, you are the first line of defense. Recognizing concussion symptoms early can significantly improve recovery outcomes. These symptoms generally fall into four categories:

Physical Red Flags

  • Headache or "pressure" in the head (the most common complaint).
  • Nausea or vomiting.
  • Balance problems or dizziness.
  • Sensitivity to light or noise.
  • Feeling sluggish, hazy, or groggy.

Cognitive and Emotional Changes

  • Difficulty concentrating or remembering.
  • Feeling "foggy" or slowed down.
  • Irritability, sadness, or becoming more emotional than usual.
  • Changes in sleep patterns (sleeping more or less than usual).
The National Institutes of Health (NIH) emphasizes that if an athlete reports any of these symptoms after a hit, they should be removed from play immediately. "When in doubt, sit them out."

The Critical Window: When to Seek Emergency Care

Most concussions are mild, but some head injuries involve internal bleeding or swelling that requires immediate intervention. You should head to the nearest Irving emergency room or urgent care if your child experiences "danger signs," such as:
  • One pupil is larger than the other.
  • Drowsiness or inability to wake up.
  • A headache that gets worse and does not go away.
  • Weakness, numbness, or decreased coordination.
  • Repeated vomiting or nausea.
  • Slurred speech or convulsions.

When to Get a CT Scan After a Hit

A common question parents ask is, "When to get a CT scan after a hit?" It is important to know that most concussions do not show up on a standard CT scan or MRI. These tests are primarily used to rule out more serious issues like skull fractures or brain bleeding. The healthcare providers typically order imaging only if there are specific neurological deficits, prolonged loss of consciousness, or worsening physical symptoms. Your provider will perform a clinical evaluation first to determine if imaging is necessary.

The Danger of Rushing Back: Secondary Impact Syndrome

The biggest risk in youth sports isn't necessarily the first concussion, it’s the second one. If an athlete returns to play before their brain has fully healed from the first injury, a second hit (even a minor one) can lead to Secondary Impact Syndrome. This is a rare but often fatal condition where the brain swells rapidly and uncontrollably. Because the adolescent brain is still developing, it is particularly vulnerable. Following a strict medical protocol ensures the brain has the metabolic energy it needs to repair itself before being put at risk again.

The Path to Recovery: Return-to-Learn and Return-to-Play Guidelines

Recovery is a marathon, not a sprint. It outlines a two-pronged approach to getting student-athletes back to their normal lives.

Step 1: Returning to the Classroom (Return-to-Learn)

Before a child can return to the field, they must be able to handle the cognitive demands of school. Thinking and learning are exercises for the brain.
  • Rest: Initially, the student may need shorter school days or frequent breaks.
  • Accommodations: They might need extra time on tests or a quiet environment to avoid light and noise triggers.
  • Progression: As concussion symptoms subside, academic workloads are gradually increased.

Step 2: Graduated Return-to-Play Protocol

Once a student is back in class and symptom-free without medication, they can begin the return-to-learn and return-to-play guidelines. This is a 5-step process supervised by a healthcare professional:
  1. Back to Light Aerobic Activity: 5–10 minutes of walking or stationary cycling. No weightlifting.
  2. Moderate Exercise: Increasing heart rate with jogging or brisk walking.
  3. Non-contact Training Drills: Adding sport-specific movements (e.g., running laps, dribbling) but no head impact.
  4. Practice: Full contact practice only after medical clearance.
  5. Return to Competition: Full game play.
Each step usually takes at least 24 hours. If any concussion symptoms return during a step, the athlete must stop and rest for a day before dropping back to the previous level.

Concussions are serious, and early intervention can make all the difference in your child's recovery. Ensure they are following proper concussion protocols for a safe return to play. Learn the signs, when to seek help, and how to support your child’s recovery journey.

If a head injury brings danger signs such as one dilated pupil, repeated vomiting, a worsening headache, slurred speech, a seizure, or trouble waking, call 911 or get emergency concussion care at ER of Irving right away. Call us now at (972) 893-3148 for immediate assistance or to speak with a healthcare professional.

Stay informed with helpful tips on recognizing a concussion and keeping your family safe. Follow ER of Irving on Facebook and Instagram for health updates.

FAQs

How long do concussion symptoms usually last? 

Most children recover within 1 to 3 weeks, though some may take longer depending on the severity and their history of previous head injuries.

Can my child sleep after a hit to the head? 

Yes. The old advice to "keep them awake" has changed. It suggests that rest is vital for recovery. However, you should monitor them for any of the "danger signs" mentioned above.

Does a helmet prevent all concussions? 

No. While helmets are essential for preventing skull fractures, they cannot stop the brain from moving inside the skull during a sudden impact.

When should I call the doctor? 

You should contact a healthcare provider for any suspected concussion. If symptoms are worsening or if the injury occurred during a high-speed impact, seek medical attention immediately.

Irritability and emotional changes are very common concussion symptoms. The brain is struggling to process information and regulate emotions while it heals.

Yes. Any "ding" that results in a change in mental status or physical symptoms is considered a concussion and should be treated seriously.

title.raw: Lower Right Abdominal Pain: Is it Appendicitis?
title.rendered: Lower Right Abdominal Pain: Is it Appendicitis?

content.raw:
Finding yourself or a loved one clutching the lower right side of the stomach can be a frightening experience. When sharp abdominal pain strikes out of nowhere, the first question that usually flashes through your mind is: "Is this appendicitis?" Because appendicitis can progress from a dull ache to a life-threatening crisis in a matter of hours, understanding the warning signs is vital for your safety. It is one of the most common reasons for emergency abdominal surgery, yet many patients hesitate to seek care, thinking they just have a bad case of indigestion or a temporary stomach virus. In this guide, we will help you distinguish between a simple stomach ache and a medical emergency. By knowing how to recognize specific appendicitis symptoms and understanding when the "wait and see" approach becomes dangerous, you can make informed decisions for your health or the health of someone you love. Our goal is to provide the clarity you need to act quickly, ensuring that a manageable condition doesn’t turn into a surgical emergency.

Is it just a Stomach Ache or Appendicitis?

Abdominal discomfort is incredibly common, often caused by something as simple as indigestion or a viral "stomach bug." Lower abdominal pressure can also point to a urinary problem such as bladder distention. However, appendicitis, an inflammation of the appendix, is a serious condition that affects about 5% to 9% of the population at some point in their lives. According to NIH, the appendix is a small, finger-shaped pouch attached to the large intestine. While its exact purpose is still debated, its ability to cause trouble is well-known. When the appendix becomes blocked or infected, bacteria multiply rapidly, leading to swelling and irritation. If left untreated, the pressure can cause the organ to burst, leading to life-threatening complications.

Identifying the Early Signs

In the beginning, appendicitis doesn't always start in the lower right side. Many patients describe a vague, dull ache near the belly button. You might feel a loss of appetite or a general sense of being "off." Because these early indicators mimic other digestive issues, it is important to monitor how the pain evolves over a few hours.

Recognizing Key Appendicitis Symptoms

According to MedlinePlus, while everyone experiences pain differently, appendicitis symptoms often follow a predictable pattern. Recognizing these signs early can be the difference between a routine procedure and a complex recovery.

The Classic "Shift" of Pain

The hallmark of appendicitis is the way the pain moves. It typically starts as a dull discomfort around the navel and then migrates toward the lower right quadrant of the abdomen. Once the pain settles there, it often becomes sharp, intense, and persistent. Unlike gas pain, which may come and go, appendicitis pain usually worsens with movement, deep breaths, coughing, or sneezing.

Fever and Nausea: The Body’s Red Flags

As the infection takes hold, your body's immune system kicks into high gear. This often triggers a low-grade fever, typically between 99°F and 100.5°F. If the fever spikes higher, it may indicate that the infection is spreading or that the appendix has perforated. Nausea and vomiting are also very common. According to the National Institutes of Health (NIH), these symptoms usually appear after the abdominal pain has started. If you experience vomiting before the pain begins, it might be more likely to be a different gastrointestinal issue, though you should still consult a provider.

Testing for Appendicitis at Home

If you are unsure whether your pain warrants an ER visit, there are specific physical signs that doctors look for. While you should never attempt to diagnose yourself, being aware of these signs can help you communicate more effectively with a healthcare professional.

Understanding the "Rebound Tenderness" Test

One of the most common clinical indicators is rebound tenderness. According to MedlinePlus, this occurs when pain is felt more intensely when pressure is released from the abdomen rather than when it is applied. To check for this, a person (or a provider) would press firmly on the lower right side of the belly and then let go quickly. If the sudden release of pressure causes a sharp jolt of pain, it suggests that the peritoneum (the lining of the abdominal cavity) is inflamed, a strong indicator of appendicitis. Important Note: Do not press forcefully on the abdomen if you suspect appendicitis, as excessive pressure could potentially worsen the condition.

When to Seek Emergency Care

Time is the most critical factor when dealing with an inflamed appendix. If you experience severe abdominal pain that makes it difficult to stand up straight or walk, you should seek medical attention immediately.

Why a Ruptured Appendix is a Surgical Emergency

The greatest danger of appendicitis is a rupture or perforation. According to NIH, if the appendix bursts, the bacteria and stool trapped inside spill into the abdominal cavity. This leads to peritonitis, a severe infection of the abdominal lining that can cause sepsis and organ failure. Interestingly, some patients feel a brief moment of relief if the appendix ruptures because the pressure is suddenly released. However, this "honeymoon period" is short-lived; within hours, the pain returns, often much worse and spread across the entire abdomen, accompanied by a high fever. NIH states that this is a true surgical emergency that requires immediate intervention and high-dose antibiotics.

What to Expect at the Clinic or ER

When you arrive at an urgent care or emergency room, the medical team will act quickly to confirm or rule out appendicitis.
  1. Physical Exam: A doctor will check for guarding (tensing the muscles) and rebound tenderness.
  2. Blood Tests: High white blood cell counts often indicate that the body is fighting an infection.
  3. Imaging: The FDA states that doctors frequently use ultrasound or CT scans to get a clear picture of the appendix.
  4. Treatment: If appendicitis is confirmed, the standard treatment is an appendectomy (surgical removal of the appendix). Thanks to modern medicine, many of these surgeries are now performed laparoscopically, using tiny incisions that allow for a faster recovery.

Is It Just a Stomach Ache or Appendicitis? Recognize the Symptoms & Know When to Seek Emergency Care

Don't Wait - Act Fast! If you're experiencing sharp abdominal pain or other signs of appendicitis, visit the ER of Irving for immediate evaluation and treatment. Our team is here 24/7 to provide expert care when you need it most. Call us now at (972) 893-3148 for immediate assistance or to speak with a healthcare professional. Stay informed with helpful tips on recognizing the warning signs of appendicitis and other abdominal emergencies. Follow ER of Irving on Facebook and Instagram for health updates.

FAQs

Can appendicitis go away on its own? 

In very rare, mild cases, inflammation may subside with antibiotics, but this is uncommon. Most cases require surgery to prevent the risk of a life-threatening rupture. 

Where exactly is the appendix located? 

The appendix is located in the lower right-hand side of your abdomen. It sits where the small intestine meets the large intestine.

Does everyone with appendicitis get a fever? 

Not always. While a low-grade fever is common, some patients, especially older adults or young children, may not develop a fever until the infection has become quite advanced.

How long do I have before my appendix bursts? 

There is no exact timeline, but a rupture can occur within 24 to 72 hours after the symptoms first begin. 

Can children get appendicitis?

Yes. In fact, appendicitis is the most common cause of emergency abdominal surgery in children. 

What does the pain feel like? 

Most patients describe it as a sharp, localized pain that feels different from a typical stomach ache.

title.raw: Pediatric Dehydration: What to Do When Your Baby Can’t Keep Liquids Down
title.rendered: Pediatric Dehydration: What to Do When Your Baby Can’t Keep Liquids Down

content.raw:
When your child is vomiting or struggling with diarrhea, the clock feels like it’s ticking faster. For infants and young children, the balance of fluids and electrolytes in their bodies is delicate. According to NIH, because their bodies are smaller, they have less of a reserve than adults do, meaning they can become dehydrated much more quickly.

Understanding Dehydration in Infants and Toddlers

Dehydration occurs when the body loses more fluid than it takes in. In children, this is most commonly caused by "stomach flu" (gastroenteritis), but it can also be a result of a high fever or even a sore throat that makes swallowing painful. According to MedlinePlus, water makes up a large percentage of a child's body weight. When they lose water, they also lose essential salts and minerals, called electrolytes, which are necessary for the heart, brain, and kidneys to function properly.

Why are children more at risk?

Children have a higher metabolic rate and a larger surface-area-to-mass ratio. This is a medical way of saying they use up water faster and lose it through their skin more easily than adults. Furthermore, an infant cannot tell you they are thirsty; they rely entirely on their caregivers to spot the subtle changes in their behavior.

Recognizing the Signs: Is My Child Dehydrated?

It can be difficult to tell the difference between a child who is just "acting sick" and one who is becoming dangerously dehydrated. Doctors typically categorize dehydration into three stages: mild, moderate, and severe.

Mild to Moderate Symptoms

According to MedlinePlus, if your child has a stomach bug but is still alert, they may be in the mild stage. Watch for these signs from MedlinePlus:
  • Fewer wet diapers: For infants, this means no wet diaper for 6 to 8 hours. For older children, it means no urination for 8 to 12 hours.
  • Dry mouth: The inside of their mouth looks sticky or dry instead of glistening with saliva.
  • Fewer tears: When they cry, you notice fewer tears than usual.
  • Increased sleepiness: They may seem a bit more tired or less interested in playing.

Red Flags: Severe Dehydration Signs

Severe dehydration is a medical emergency. If you notice any of the following, seek immediate care at an emergency room:
  • Sunken Fontanelle: The soft spot on the top of an infant’s head appears "caved in" or sunken.
  • Sunken Eyes: Their eyes may look dark or hollow.
  • Extreme Lethargy: The child is very drowsy and difficult to wake up.
  • Skin Turgor: If you gently pinch the skin on their abdomen, it does not "snap" back quickly but stays tented.
  • Rapid Heartbeat or Breathing: Their body is working overtime to compensate for the low fluid volume.

Common Causes of Fluid Loss in Children

NIH states that the most frequent culprit is viral gastroenteritis, often referred to as the stomach flu. This can cause both vomiting and diarrhea simultaneously, which is a "double hit" to a child’s fluid levels. Other causes include:
  • High Fever: Fever leads to increased sweating and faster breathing, both of which deplete fluids.
  • Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease: Painful mouth sores can make a child refuse to drink.
  • Heat Exhaustion: Especially during summer months or heavy play.

Dehydration Symptoms in Kids and When to Take Notice During World Cup 2026

With watch parties, fan festivals, and long days in the summer heat, children can lose fluids faster than parents expect, and young children are more likely to become dehydrated than adults. Since kids don't always say when they need water, it helps to know the signs. In infants and young children, watch for a dry mouth and tongue, crying without tears, no wet diaper for three or more hours, unusual sleepiness or irritability, sunken eyes, or a high fever. These can come on quickly on hot, active days.

Managing Dehydration at Home: The Small Sips Method

If your child is vomiting but is still alert and doesn't have "red flag" symptoms, you can often manage their recovery at home. The secret is "slow and low." If a child gulps down a full bottle or a large glass of water after vomiting, their irritated stomach will likely reject it immediately. Instead, use the Small Sips Method:
  1. Wait: After your child vomits, give their stomach a rest for about 30 to 60 minutes.
  2. Teaspoon amounts: Offer 1 to 2 teaspoons (5-10 ml) of fluid every 5 to 10 minutes.
  3. Increase slowly: If they keep those small amounts down for an hour, you can gradually increase the amount.

What about Oral Rehydration Solutions (ORS)?

For pediatric dehydration, plain water isn't always enough because it lacks electrolytes. The NIH and other health authorities recommend Oral Rehydration Solutions (ORS) like Pedialyte. These are specifically balanced with the right ratio of sugar and salt to optimize absorption in the gut. A Note on Other Liquids: Avoid giving your baby apple juice, soda, or sports drinks during a bout of dehydration. The high sugar content in these drinks can actually make diarrhea worse.

When to Seek Emergency Medical Care

Sometimes, despite your best efforts, your child cannot stay hydrated at home. You should call your pediatrician or head to an urgent care center if:
  • The vomiting lasts for more than 24 hours.
  • Your child has a high fever (over 102°F or as directed by your doctor).
  • There is blood in their stool or vomit.
  • They are unable to keep even small sips of ORS down.
  • You see any signs of severe dehydration (sunken soft spot, no tears, lethargy).
In a clinical setting, healthcare providers may use Intravenous (IV) Rehydration. This delivers fluids and electrolytes directly into the bloodstream, bypassing the upset stomach entirely and providing rapid relief.

Prevention: Keeping Your Child Hydrated During Illness

Prevention starts the moment you notice the first signs of illness.
  • Don't wait for thirst: Encourage fluids early and often.
  • Keep ORS stocked: Have unflavored oral rehydration solutions in your medicine cabinet before the flu season hits.
  • Monitor Output: Keep a simple log of how many wet diapers your baby has and how many times they have vomited or had diarrhea. This information is incredibly helpful for doctors if you do need to seek care.

When Your Baby Can’t Keep Liquids Down, Trust Your Gut

If your baby or child can’t keep liquids down, is vomiting repeatedly, has diarrhea, or is not having wet diapers like usual, treat it seriously. Dehydration can worsen quickly. If you notice extreme sleepiness, no tears, a sunken soft spot, or they’re not improving despite small sips/ORS, consider it an emergency. For quick evaluation and treatment (including IV fluids if needed), head to your nearest emergency room ER of Irving is here when you need urgent, professional care. FAQs

Can I give my baby water if they are dehydrated? 

While older children can have water, infants under 6 months should generally stick to breast milk, formula, or an ORS as directed by a doctor. Plain water can dilute an infant's sodium levels if given in large amounts.

How many wet diapers should my baby have? 

Typically, a healthy infant should have at least 6 wet diapers in 24 hours. If they have had fewer than 3 or 4 in a day, it’s time to call the pediatrician.

Is ginger ale good for a vomiting child? 

No. Most sodas are too high in sugar and lack the necessary electrolytes to treat clinical dehydration. Stick to pediatric rehydration solutions.

What is a "sunken soft spot"? 

The fontanelle is the soft area on an infant's head where the skull bones haven't fused yet. When a baby is severely dehydrated, the fluid pressure drops, causing this spot to look noticeably indented.

How long does it take for a child to get dehydrated? 

In cases of severe vomiting and diarrhea, a small child can become dehydrated in as little as 12 to 24 hours.

Can I make my own rehydration solution at home? 

It is safer to use commercially prepared ORS. Home recipes can have incorrect ratios of salt and sugar, which can be dangerous for small infants.

"Is it safe to bring my baby to a summer World Cup match?"

Plenty of families do, and the key is remembering that the heat is mostly on the way in and out, not in your seat. The stadium bowl is air-conditioned and comfortable. Since infants and young children rely on the adults around them to stay cool and hydrated and lose fluid more quickly than adults, a little planning around the hot parts, parking, lines, and the walk makes the day much smoother.

"Can I bring milk or water through security for my baby?"

Stadium bag and liquid rules are strict and set by the venue, but most large stadiums make exceptions for baby formula, breast milk, and medical items. Check the official venue bag policy before you leave so you can pack what your child needs without surprises at the gate.

"How do I keep my baby hydrated while we wait in those long outdoor lines?"

Offer small, frequent feeds or sips instead of waiting for your child to seem thirsty. Giving children fluids before, during, and after time in the heat, and it recommends staying in the shade and taking breaks when you can.

"It feels freezing inside after the heat. What should I bring?"

The seating bowl is kept cool, around the low 70s, which can feel like a big swing after a hot walk in. A light layer or blanket helps your child settle, and the cool air is actually a good chance to offer a calm feed and let them recover from the heat outside.

"How will I know if the heat got to my little one, and when should we get care?"

Watch for the signs covered earlier in this post: fewer wet diapers, a dry mouth, fewer tears, unusual sleepiness or fussiness, or a sunken soft spot since children can lose fluid quickly on hot days. Move to a cool spot and offer small, frequent sips. If your child cannot keep fluids down or you see signs of severe dehydration, follow the when-to-seek-care guidance above, and the team at ER of Irving is here if you need a hand.

When your child is vomiting or struggling with diarrhea, the clock feels like it’s ticking faster. For infants and young children, the balance of fluids and electrolytes in their bodies is delicate. According to NIH, because their bodies are smaller, they have less of a reserve than adults do, meaning they can become dehydrated much more quickly.

Understanding Dehydration in Infants and Toddlers

Dehydration occurs when the body loses more fluid than it takes in. In children, this is most commonly caused by “stomach flu” (gastroenteritis), but it can also be a result of a high fever or even a sore throat that makes swallowing painful.

According to MedlinePlus, water makes up a large percentage of a child’s body weight. When they lose water, they also lose essential salts and minerals, called electrolytes, which are necessary for the heart, brain, and kidneys to function properly.

Why are children more at risk?

Children have a higher metabolic rate and a larger surface-area-to-mass ratio. This is a medical way of saying they use up water faster and lose it through their skin more easily than adults. Furthermore, an infant cannot tell you they are thirsty; they rely entirely on their caregivers to spot the subtle changes in their behavior.

Recognizing the Signs: Is My Child Dehydrated?

It can be difficult to tell the difference between a child who is just “acting sick” and one who is becoming dangerously dehydrated. Doctors typically categorize dehydration into three stages: mild, moderate, and severe.

Mild to Moderate Symptoms

According to MedlinePlus, if your child has a stomach bug but is still alert, they may be in the mild stage. Watch for these signs from MedlinePlus:

  • Fewer wet diapers: For infants, this means no wet diaper for 6 to 8 hours. For older children, it means no urination for 8 to 12 hours.
  • Dry mouth: The inside of their mouth looks sticky or dry instead of glistening with saliva.
  • Fewer tears: When they cry, you notice fewer tears than usual.
  • Increased sleepiness: They may seem a bit more tired or less interested in playing.

Red Flags: Severe Dehydration Signs

Severe dehydration is a medical emergency. If you notice any of the following, seek immediate care at an emergency room:

  • Sunken Fontanelle: The soft spot on the top of an infant’s head appears “caved in” or sunken.
  • Sunken Eyes: Their eyes may look dark or hollow.
  • Extreme Lethargy: The child is very drowsy and difficult to wake up.
  • Skin Turgor: If you gently pinch the skin on their abdomen, it does not “snap” back quickly but stays tented.
  • Rapid Heartbeat or Breathing: Their body is working overtime to compensate for the low fluid volume.

Common Causes of Fluid Loss in Children

NIH states that the most frequent culprit is viral gastroenteritis, often referred to as the stomach flu. This can cause both vomiting and diarrhea simultaneously, which is a “double hit” to a child’s fluid levels.

Other causes include:

  • High Fever: Fever leads to increased sweating and faster breathing, both of which deplete fluids.
  • Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease: Painful mouth sores can make a child refuse to drink.
  • Heat Exhaustion: Especially during summer months or heavy play.

Dehydration Symptoms in Kids and When to Take Notice During World Cup 2026

With watch parties, fan festivals, and long days in the summer heat, children can lose fluids faster than parents expect, and young children are more likely to become dehydrated than adults. Since kids don’t always say when they need water, it helps to know the signs. In infants and young children, watch for a dry mouth and tongue, crying without tears, no wet diaper for three or more hours, unusual sleepiness or irritability, sunken eyes, or a high fever. These can come on quickly on hot, active days.

Managing Dehydration at Home: The Small Sips Method

If your child is vomiting but is still alert and doesn’t have “red flag” symptoms, you can often manage their recovery at home. The secret is “slow and low.”

If a child gulps down a full bottle or a large glass of water after vomiting, their irritated stomach will likely reject it immediately. Instead, use the Small Sips Method:

  1. Wait: After your child vomits, give their stomach a rest for about 30 to 60 minutes.
  2. Teaspoon amounts: Offer 1 to 2 teaspoons (5-10 ml) of fluid every 5 to 10 minutes.
  3. Increase slowly: If they keep those small amounts down for an hour, you can gradually increase the amount.

What about Oral Rehydration Solutions (ORS)?

For pediatric dehydration, plain water isn’t always enough because it lacks electrolytes. The NIH and other health authorities recommend Oral Rehydration Solutions (ORS) like Pedialyte. These are specifically balanced with the right ratio of sugar and salt to optimize absorption in the gut.

A Note on Other Liquids: Avoid giving your baby apple juice, soda, or sports drinks during a bout of dehydration. The high sugar content in these drinks can actually make diarrhea worse.

When to Seek Emergency Medical Care

Sometimes, despite your best efforts, your child cannot stay hydrated at home. You should call your pediatrician or head to an urgent care center if:

  • The vomiting lasts for more than 24 hours.
  • Your child has a high fever (over 102°F or as directed by your doctor).
  • There is blood in their stool or vomit.
  • They are unable to keep even small sips of ORS down.
  • You see any signs of severe dehydration (sunken soft spot, no tears, lethargy).

In a clinical setting, healthcare providers may use Intravenous (IV) Rehydration. This delivers fluids and electrolytes directly into the bloodstream, bypassing the upset stomach entirely and providing rapid relief.

Prevention: Keeping Your Child Hydrated During Illness

Prevention starts the moment you notice the first signs of illness.

  • Don’t wait for thirst: Encourage fluids early and often.
  • Keep ORS stocked: Have unflavored oral rehydration solutions in your medicine cabinet before the flu season hits.
  • Monitor Output: Keep a simple log of how many wet diapers your baby has and how many times they have vomited or had diarrhea. This information is incredibly helpful for doctors if you do need to seek care.

When Your Baby Can’t Keep Liquids Down, Trust Your Gut

If your baby or child can’t keep liquids down, is vomiting repeatedly, has diarrhea, or is not having wet diapers like usual, treat it seriously. Dehydration can worsen quickly. If you notice extreme sleepiness, no tears, a sunken soft spot, or they’re not improving despite small sips/ORS, consider it an emergency.
